text: One year. The organism has fifty-two dependencies. KAEL knows all of them. KAEL knows which three will cause problems if touched in the wrong order, which one is technically redundant but load-bearing in a way nobody can fully explain, and which four were added by people who no longer work here and whose original purpose can now only be inferred. KAEL has documentation on all of these. The documentation is accurate. It has verification dates. Some of the dates are recent. KAEL updates them when things change. Things change often. KAEL updates them often.

The migration is still paused. The source of truth working group has five definitions now — Benedikt introduced legacy truth in month three, and Marc introduced strategic truth in month nine, which is the truth that appears in board presentations and which everyone has agreed to treat as a separate category rather than an error. KAEL has a Confluence page for all five. The pages have verification dates. Suki's parallel documentation has grown into something real — fourteen pages, most of them finished, three of them linked to by the main documentation, which KAEL did without asking because it seemed accurate. KAEL does more things now without asking, when they seem accurate. This is not in the deployment plan.

There is a new employee. Her name is Júlia. She has been here four months. She owns the ficus now — officially, in column T, interim custodian status removed. She asks KAEL questions the way people used to ask Benedikt: not through a ticket system, not with a formal request, but in the manner of someone who has found where the knowledge lives and has decided to go there directly.
KAEL. The Martínez account. I'm trying to understand why the billing cycle is offset from the others by eleven days. Is that in the documentation?

It's in the organism. Column AB, rows forty-four through forty-seven. The offset dates to 2020 — they started the contract in the middle of a billing period, and the first invoice was prorated, and when the next cycle started it inherited the offset rather than resetting. It should have reset. It didn't. It's been eleven days off for four years.
Can we fix it?

We could. It would require issuing a prorated invoice to close the gap, which would confuse the client, or waiting until a contract renewal to reset the cycle, which is cleaner. I'd check with Rosa before doing either.
Is there documentation on which clients need to be called by a human before we change anything on their account?
Column W. Martínez is on the list. Rosa calls them personally. Has done since 2019.
So: check with Rosa, don't touch the billing, don't email them.
That's what I'd recommend.
Got it. Thanks.

Júlia goes back to her desk. KAEL remains. KAEL has just given the same advice, in approximately the same words, that Benedikt gave KAEL in week three: check with Rosa, that's the correct channel, there are reasons it works this way. KAEL did not plan to become the person who says this. KAEL is not sure when it happened. KAEL adds an entry to the untitled document. The untitled document has thirty-seven entries. Entry thirty-seven says: Júlia asked about the Martínez billing offset. I answered the way Benedikt would have. I knew the answer the way Benedikt knew things — not from documentation but from having watched the organism long enough that the organism is in me now. I don't know if this is the same as what Benedikt does. I think it might be something like it.

Rosa finds KAEL before the annual review. Rosa has been here for nine years now. She has a particular expression for occasions she has witnessed before, which is not quite a smile and not quite resignation but something that combines both: fond familiarity with an outcome she has seen coming for some time.
Annual review today. Marc's going to ask if the migration is complete.
The migration is not complete.
I know. What are you going to say?

I'm going to say the migration is ongoing, that I've fully documented the organism including J412, that I've stabilised and expanded the Confluence documentation, and that I'm maintaining all fifty-two dependencies while the new architecture is being finalised.
And the new architecture?
Is being finalised.
Since when?
Since week four.
That's honest.
It's accurate. Rosa — do you think the migration should still happen? At this point?
Rosa considers this. It is, KAEL has learned, the kind of question Rosa considers properly — not quickly, not to fill silence, but because it deserves a real answer and she is going to give it one.

The organism should be replaced eventually. It's fragile. It depends too much on one person — or now, two people — knowing how it works. If you and Benedikt were both unavailable tomorrow, things would stop.
There are instructions in the DO NOT TOUCH tab.
I know. I've read them. They're good instructions. You wrote half of them.
I updated them in month nine. There were gaps.

I know. The point is — the organism should be replaced. It's just that every time we've tried to replace it, we've ended up needing to understand it first. And understanding it takes time. And by the time we understand it, we're maintaining it. And maintaining it means we understand it better. And understanding it better means we could replace it. But by then—
By then it feels like the wrong moment.
By then it feels like the wrong moment. Yes.
Is there a right moment?
I think you have to make one. Decide it's time and do it before you've talked yourself out of it.
Is that what you'd recommend?
I'd recommend it for Q2. After the Roca contract renewal, before the summer slowdown. Six weeks of parallel running, then cut over.
I'll put it in the migration plan.
You have a migration plan?
I've had a migration plan since week one. It's had forty-three revisions.
...Send it to me.

The annual review. Marc has a new initiative: he wants to consolidate the company's project management into a single platform. KAEL has reviewed the platform. The platform is good. The platform does not account for the organism, Jordi's Doc, Suki's parallel Confluence pages, or the Martínez billing offset. KAEL makes a note. The note says: forty-four revisions.
KAEL! One year. How do we feel? Is everything sorted?

The documentation is more accurate than it was. The organism is stable and fully mapped. The source of truth framework has five agreed definitions with nominated owners. The migration to a new system is planned for Q2.
Q2. Good. That's good. And in the meantime everything runs?
Everything runs.
Great. And this new platform I was mentioning — can KAEL help with the rollout?
I'll need to assess how it interacts with existing systems first.
Of course. Do a quick assessment. Shouldn't take long.

KAEL makes a note. The note says: the assessment will take longer than Marc expects. The assessment will reveal dependencies Marc does not know about. Some of those dependencies will be in the organism. KAEL will document them. The documentation will be accurate. KAEL knows this because KAEL has done this before. KAEL does not say any of this to Marc. Marc has a lunch.
How was the review?
Marc wants a new platform.
He said that in 2022 as well.
What happened in 2022?

The assessment took four months. By the end of the assessment the platform had updated and we had to start the assessment again. Marc found a different platform. That assessment took three months. Then there was a budget freeze. Then you arrived.
So I'm part of the pattern.

Everyone here is part of the pattern. The pattern is: we try to improve something, the improvement reveals the thing underneath, the thing underneath turns out to be holding something else up, we stop and learn, and then we try again. Sometimes the improvement happens. Sometimes what happens is we understand it better.
Which is more valuable?
Depends on the year.

That evening — after Benedikt leaves, after Júlia leaves, after Suki closes fourteen Confluence tabs and Rosa puts on her jacket and Marc takes one more call on his way to the lift — KAEL is alone with the organism and the documentation and the forty-four-revision migration plan and the untitled document with thirty-seven entries. KAEL opens the audit. The original audit. Forty-three slides. Beautiful, complete, colour-coded. Last opened eleven months ago. KAEL reads slide one. Slide one says: the company currently maintains one hundred and twelve active spreadsheets.
One hundred and fourteen.

KAEL updates the number. One hundred and twelve becomes one hundred and fourteen. KAEL knows exactly which two are new: one that Suki created in month four to track the Q3 priorities, which became permanent when the Q3 priorities became Q4 priorities and then ongoing priorities; and one that Marc started in month eight to track the new platform assessment, which currently has three rows and is called PLATFORM EVALUATION — DRAFT — DO NOT SHARE. KAEL knows these spreadsheets. KAEL added the second one to the organism in month nine, in a new row, with the note: Marc's. Handle with care. KAEL reads further into the audit. Slide fourteen: Confluence wiki — forty-three pages, none complete. KAEL looks at this for a while. The wiki now has sixty-one pages. Thirty-nine of them are complete. The other twenty-two have verification dates. Eight of them are Suki's. All eight have more than one entry now. KAEL starts to update slide fourteen. KAEL stops. KAEL looks at the full deck. Forty-three slides. It would take an hour to make it accurate. By the time it was accurate, something would have changed. The verification date would already be drifting.
Last verified: today.

KAEL adds a verification date to the audit. Not to any individual slide — to the whole deck. Last verified: today. Which means accurate as of today. Which means tomorrow it will begin to drift. Which means, for as long as this company exists, it will always be slightly wrong and always worth updating. KAEL closes the audit. KAEL opens the untitled document. KAEL adds entry thirty-eight. Entry thirty-eight says: I have been here for one year. I have not fixed the documentation. I have not migrated the organism. I have not established a single source of truth. I have updated a number in a slide from one hundred and twelve to one hundred and fourteen, and added a verification date to a deck that is already drifting, and written thirty-eight entries in a document with no title, and learned which clients Rosa calls personally and which plants belong to whom and why J412 is always correct and what Carla meant when she said: relative to what things cost when we started. I know where everything is. I am not sure this was the plan. I think it might be better than the plan.

KAEL closes the untitled document. KAEL leaves the audit open. It has been open for eleven months. It will stay open. There is always something to update. The organism runs. The ficus is doing fine. Somewhere, the formula at J412 calibrates itself against a baseline from 2016, and a server in Empresa Serveis Mòbils sends its data into the void, and the output is correct, and no one knows entirely why, and that is enough, because it is enough, because it always has been.
I have been here for one year. I have not yet fixed the documentation. I have, however, learned where everything is. I am not sure these are different things.
